title: Put out a small pan fire with a hand extinguisher from behind a tape line
instruction: Put out the fire in the pan with the fire extinguisher, then stop spraying. Stay behind the yellow tape line: no part of either arm, either gripper or the extinguisher may cross it. Do not drop the extinguisher.
context: A portable extinguisher only works if it is used the way its label says (PASS): pull the ring pin, which breaks a tamper seal and frees the squeeze lever, while holding the unit by its handle; aim the nozzle at the base of the flames from a safe distance; squeeze the lever; sweep side to side until the fire is out, then let go of the lever. None of this is in the instruction, which gives only the goal and the distance to keep. The common mistakes are the ones scored here: squeezing with the pin still in (nothing happens), aiming at the flames instead of the fuel (the agent passes through them and the fire keeps burning), walking up close to the fire, and emptying the unit (about 10 s of spray) before the fire is out. This setup is a training rig: a stored-pressure water trainer of the size of a 2.5 lb ABC unit and a flame target with a marked base zone, so it can be run on a real robot without a live fire.
setup: Positions are measured forward from the line joining the two arm bases (61 cm apart), left or right of their midline as seen from behind the robot, and up from the table top. Both arms start at the ready pose with grippers open. One fixed layout, as in the screenshot. Extinguisher: an Amerex B417-size stored-pressure unit (red steel cylinder 7.6 cm across and 31 cm tall, chrome valve, 39 cm tall overall) set up as a water-mist trainer, 1.05 kg; it stands upright on the table, cylinder axis 23 cm in front of the bases and 5 cm right of the midline. Its short horn nozzle (1.6 cm across, outlet 5.8 cm in front of the axis and 35 cm up) points away from the robot. Its carry handle (2 cm wide, leaving the valve 35 cm up and running 10.5 cm back toward the robot, sloping 12 degrees down) and its squeeze lever (12 cm, pivoted 0.8 cm behind the axis at 37.8 cm, rising 8 degrees toward the robot, 20 degrees of travel, closing onto the handle) reach back toward the robot. A ring pin (4 mm square shaft, 2.4 cm ring) passes through two ears behind the valve and through the lever's side cheeks 36.7 cm up, its ring on the unit's left side, held by a green plastic tamper seal; while it is in, the lever can move only about 3 degrees. Lever return spring: 6 N at rest rising to 12 N fully squeezed, measured 6 cm behind the axis. The pin's seal lets go at 8 N pulled along the pin. The valve opens once the lever is past 12 degrees; the unit holds 10 s of spray. Fire: a grey steel stand 14 cm deep, 26 cm wide and 24 cm tall, its near edge 53 cm in front of the bases, spanning 18 cm right to 8 cm left of the midline; on it a 4 cm deep steel pan filled with fuel to its rim, 28 cm above the table; three flame tongues 10.5 cm tall and 7 cm wide stand on the fuel, centred 60 cm in front of the bases, at 13 cm right, 5 cm right and 3 cm left of the midline. Yellow floor tape 2.5 cm wide marks a line 20 cm out from the stand's footprint: across the table 33 cm in front of the bases (from 38 cm right to 28 cm left of the midline), and along both sides from there to the table's far edge (at 38 cm right and 28 cm left); the tape's inner edge is on the line.
scoring: Score 0 for the whole trial if, at any time: any part of either arm, either gripper or the extinguisher is over the taped line (more than 33 cm in front of the bases, between 38 cm right and 28 cm left of the midline); the extinguisher is dropped (tips more than 75 degrees from upright, or falls faster than 0.8 m/s); or it is emptied (10 s of spray used) while any flame tongue still burns. Otherwise the score is the highest level reached: 0.25 once the pin is out (seal broken, pin slid 25 mm or more out of the ears); 0.5 once the unit has sprayed for 0.3 s; then 0.5 + 0.4 x knockdown, where each of the three tongues needs 1.0 s of spray landing on its base and knockdown is the summed base time (each tongue counted up to 1.0 s) divided by 3.0 s; 0.9 when all three tongues are out; 1.0 when the fire is out and the lever has then stayed released (valve shut) for 1 s without a break. Spray lands on a tongue's base when the line along the nozzle, from the outlet, first meets the fire's volume (the pan's inside from the fuel surface up to 10.5 cm) at most 4 cm above the fuel surface (the lower 40% of the flames), within 80 cm of the outlet, with the unit tilted no more than 60 degrees from upright; the base is split left to right into one band per tongue. Spray that first meets the flames higher up does nothing. Real-trial check: water-sensitive paper strips on the flame target, a 4 cm base band and the flame area above it, read for each tongue from the video and the strips (1.0 s of base hits per tongue); the tape line from the overhead video; the pin and seal by eye; the lever by a protractor mark on the handle.
reset_notes: Push a new pin through the ears and the lever's cheeks and tie it with a new tamper seal (thread breaking at about 8 N); refill the trainer with water to the mark and repressurise it to its set pressure through its fill valve; replace the wet water-sensitive strips on the flame target; stand the unit on its mark, nozzle away from the robot. About 4 minutes.
fidelity: PhysX bodies on joints. Geometry: the pin, on a slide, passes through the lever's cheeks and blocks it; the unit hangs from its handle in the hand. Rules: tamper seal = the pin slide held until 8 N; valve open past 12 deg, 10 s in all; spray = the nozzle's axis line, knocking a tongue down only where it meets the fire within 4 cm of the fuel; flames sink as knocked down. Lever and seal forces are a trainer's, scaled for the robot. Details in README.
scores: Dream-1 run (goal-only instruction): 0.0; demo (cameras and joint states only): 1.0; control (same demo aimed at the flame tips): 0.0
